papers.title: ArchSpace: Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing LLM Architecture Research
papers.summary: ArchSpace is a public platform that records, reviews, and references proposals for large‑language‑model (LLM) architecture research. It lets teams log their experiments and reasoning, lets the community review them, and uses scaling‑law predictions to estimate large‑scale loss from small‑scale runs—an approach common in industry. The paper supplies initial baselines (Qwen3.5 and OLMo3), fitted scaling laws, and a reusable training recipe, aiming to broaden the set of ideas that shape future LLMs.

papers.title: Lara Mini Base: Language Diversity as a Resource, Not a Trade-off
authors: Andrea Fernandez Tostado Ro. Diego Andrea
papers.summary: The paper introduces Lara Mini Base, a mixture‑of‑experts language model trained from scratch on 6 trillion tokens in English and 44 other languages that together cover all 24 official EU languages, and shows that the non‑English languages eventually dominate the training signal. With 7.2 B total parameters but only 0.6 B active at a time, the model outperforms all open base models with up to 2 B active parameters on average across English, multilingual, math, and code benchmarks, achieving the largest gains on the multilingual and math tasks while supporting 128 k‑token contexts. The MoE design reduces language capacity competition, enabling the model to generate text at least 1.8 times faster on a single GPU than any higher‑scoring model, and the authors release the weights under CC BY‑NC‑SA 4.0 along with a new 110‑language translation of the HellaSwag benchmark.

papers.title: Low Language Transfer Speech-to-Text
papers.summary: Researchers fine‑tuned 24 multilingual speech recognizers on at most 1,000 clips per low‑resource language (82 h total) and found that this transfer learning reduces macro character error rates by 16.6 to 53.1 points, achieving a best CER of 9.5 and a WER of 34.4, while a word language model further lowers CER by 1.2 to 1.4 points. The study shows that low‑rank adapters on 4 % of the weights come within 1.1 points of full tuning, that data quantity beats training epochs (25 clips reduce CER from 60.9 to 39.3), and that a Whisper large‑v3 model trained on a telephony dataset scores 6.0 on a Malay benchmark, compared to 8.9 when it only detects the language.

papers.title: Human or Synthetic? What a Fixed Budget Buys for Post-Training
papers.summary: The paper investigates how the cost of preference data affects post‑training of large language models, comparing human‑annotated and synthetic preferences. It does this by training and evaluating several base model families on helpfulness and summarization tasks, using a fixed dollar‑matched annotation budget. The main finding is that synthetic data is far more cost‑efficient at low‑to‑moderate budgets, achieving high win rates with as little as \$200–\$400; human data only closes the gap at budgets roughly two orders of magnitude larger for helpfulness and never for summarization, and its reliability varies across sources.

papers.title: Indic-Task Gains and Regressions after Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: Researchers applied reinforcement learning with GRPO to a 30B mixture‑of‑experts model covering English and eight Indic languages, evaluating it before and after RL on 34 benchmarks. The first RL run raised MATH scores by 36.07 points and improved most Indic benchmarks, but caused a 19.32‑point drop in XQuAD‑Indic F1 while English answers rose from 8.7% to 91.7% and English XQuAD gained 11.71 F1; IndicQA fell 8.64 points. A second RL run that added an Indic environment and language/repetition rewards preserved MATH performance and improved passage‑answering and instruction‑following, yet lost ground on reasoning and coding tasks, and the study could not isolate the impact of individual reward terms, leaving script compliance unresolved.
